title: Caring and Organizing Both Count
text:
In the late 1940s and 1950s, researchers at Ohio State University asked employees to describe their supervisors and found two broad themes. Consideration meant showing concern and respect for followers, looking out for their welfare and expressing appreciation. Initiating structure meant organizing the work: defining roles, setting goals and standards, and making sure tasks were done.

For a time these two dimensions dominated leadership research, but by the 1980s many scholars had dismissed them as outdated and inconsistent. In 2004 Timothy Judge, Ronald Piccolo and Remus Ilies decided to check whether that dismissal was fair. They combined the results of more than a hundred earlier studies.

Both dimensions turned out to be solidly related to effective leadership. Consideration was strongly linked to followers' satisfaction with the leader and with their job, to their motivation and to how effective the leader was seen to be. Initiating structure was more closely related to the performance of the leader and the group. The authors concluded that the old dimensions had been abandoned too soon.
lesson: Good leaders do two jobs at once: they care about people and they organize the work. Neglect either one and the team suffers.
people: Timothy Judge, Ronald Piccolo, Remus Ilies
source: Judge, T. A., Piccolo, R. F., and Ilies, R. (2004). The forgotten ones? The validity of consideration and initiating structure in leadership research. Journal of Applied Psychology, 89(1), 36-51.
